episode_title: The Human Skills That Make or Break a Project Manager | Ep. 13
question: What is the core difference between managing under pressure and leading under pressure in project management?
transcript_excerpt: Managing under pressure means you are doing okay yourself, but leading under pressure means that you are helping everyone else get through that phase as well. The distinction is critical because as a project manager, you need to remain calm and provide clarity and direction to your team even when facing severe financial, time, personnel, or third-party pressures.

episode_title: The Human Skills That Make or Break a Project Manager | Ep. 13
question: How has the role of project manager evolved from the 1950s to today?
transcript_excerpt: Project managers were originally the most senior technical person with deep expertise in the specific field, such as a senior bridge engineer managing bridge construction. Over 70 years, the role shifted to being an expert in stakeholder engagement, communication, and soft skills rather than technical expertise. The discipline moved from accidental project managers, who shuffled into the role after reaching technical mastery, to intentional project managers who actively choose and study project management as a desirable career.

episode_title: The Human Skills That Make or Break a Project Manager | Ep. 13
question: Why is technical skill alone insufficient to make an effective project manager?
transcript_excerpt: Technical skills are fundamental and everyone needs them, including understanding time, cost, quality, risk, and procurement. However, having technical skills does not make you a good project manager; it only makes you able to understand project management. If you can get on with people, build teams, take people on a journey with you, and motivate people, that is what truly makes the difference and creates outcomes beyond just deliverables.

episode_title: The Human Skills That Make or Break a Project Manager | Ep. 13
question: What role does VUCA play in explaining why soft skills now matter more than technical expertise in projects?
transcript_excerpt: VUCA stands for volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity. Projects now suffer from VUCA because of constantly shifting landscapes and contexts. The impact of VUCA means technical expertise is secondary to the ability to navigate uncertain, complex environments. This requires soft skills, flexibility, adaptability, and sharing information with people in a way that does not panic them but instead acknowledges issues and demonstrates that the team is trying to deal with them.

episode_title: The Human Skills That Make or Break a Project Manager | Ep. 13
question: How should project managers approach problem-solving when issues arise under stress rather than reacting immediately?
transcript_excerpt: When things get stressful in projects, the automatic reaction is to deal with the problem immediately. However, like the risk management process which identifies and assesses risks before dealing with them, project managers should give themselves a moment to be calm, clear, and concise in understanding what the real problem is. This prevents creating additional knock-on problems. Taking a moment to breathe and separating your ego—your perception of self—allows you to step back from the swirling situation and provide clarity and direction to others.

episode_title: The Human Skills That Make or Break a Project Manager | Ep. 13
question: What is the difference between knowledge and skills in project management, and why does this distinction matter?
transcript_excerpt: Knowledge is what the project manager knows about project management concepts and frameworks. Skills are the ability to put that knowledge into effect with a team. It is not necessarily what the project manager knows that makes the difference; it is how they can work with the team. This shift from knowledge to skills represents the broader movement from technical discipline to leader of people discipline.

episode_title: The Human Skills That Make or Break a Project Manager | Ep. 13
question: Should capability or experience be the primary criterion for assessing whether someone can be an effective project manager?
transcript_excerpt: Experience is not the best indicator of successful projects. A highly competent project manager with strong capability could work on any project, whereas experience is project-specific. While specialized technical knowledge may be needed for critical projects like nuclear power plants, outside of such specialties, capability in project management should transfer across infrastructure, banking, communications, and other fields. Capability should be prioritized over years of experience.

episode_title: The Human Skills That Make or Break a Project Manager | Ep. 13
question: How can project managers help their teams navigate problems and uncertainty without causing panic or denial?
transcript_excerpt: Rather than flat-out denying a problem, a good project manager should acknowledge the concern and work through it patiently with the team, similar to checking for a monster under a bed with a torch and involving the child in the process. This approach brings the team along the journey so they reach the same understanding. It involves taking time, checking all areas, and moving forward together rather than denying the problem, which will resurface elsewhere and cause greater issues later.
